truth: 1. A prime number is a whole number greater than one with exactly two divisors.
2. Those two divisors are always the number one and the number itself.
3. The smallest prime number is two, which is also the only even prime.
4. Every other even number is divisible by two and therefore cannot be prime.
5. The first few primes are two, three, five, seven, eleven, and thirteen.
6. A whole number greater than one that is not prime is called composite.
7. The number one is neither prime nor composite by modern convention.
8. Excluding one from the primes keeps many important theorems simple and clean.
9. The fundamental theorem of arithmetic describes how integers decompose into primes.
10. It states that every integer above one factors into primes in essentially one way.
11. Essentially one way means the factorization is unique apart from the order of factors.
12. For example, sixty equals two times two times three times five.
13. No other collection of primes multiplies together to give exactly sixty.
14. This uniqueness is why primes are often called the atoms of arithmetic.
15. Euclid proved more than two thousand years ago that there are infinitely many primes.
16. His argument begins by assuming that only finitely many primes exist.
17. He then multiplies all of those supposed primes together and adds one.
18. The resulting number leaves remainder one when divided by any prime on the list.
19. Therefore its prime factors must be missing from the supposedly complete list.
20. This contradiction shows that no finite list can contain every prime.
21. Euclid's proof remains one of the most admired arguments in all of mathematics.
22. The sieve of Eratosthenes is an ancient method for listing primes efficiently.
23. To use it, write down the integers from two up to some chosen limit.
24. Circle two, then cross out every larger multiple of two on the list.
25. Move to the next uncrossed number, which is three, and circle it.
26. Cross out every larger multiple of three that still remains uncrossed.
27. Repeat this process with each new uncrossed number you encounter.
28. The circled numbers that remain at the end are exactly the primes.
29. You only need to sieve with primes up to the square root of the limit.
30. That shortcut works because every composite has a factor no larger than its square root.
31. Trial division tests whether a number is prime by checking possible divisors directly.
32. Like the sieve, trial division only needs to check divisors up to the square root.
33. For very large numbers, trial division becomes far too slow to be practical.
34. Modern computers use cleverer tests to decide primality for enormous numbers.
35. The greatest common divisor of two integers is the largest number dividing both.
36. For instance, the greatest common divisor of twelve and eighteen is six.
37. Two integers are called coprime when their greatest common divisor equals one.
38. Eight and fifteen are coprime even though neither of them is prime.
39. The Euclidean algorithm computes greatest common divisors quickly and reliably.
40. It repeatedly replaces the larger number with its remainder after division by the smaller.
41. When the remainder finally becomes zero, the last nonzero remainder is the answer.
42. Starting from forty-eight and eighteen, the remainders are twelve, six, and zero.
43. So the greatest common divisor of forty-eight and eighteen is six.
44. The algorithm runs in a number of steps proportional to the digits involved.
45. Bezout's identity says the greatest common divisor is a combination of the two numbers.
46. Specifically, there exist integers x and y with ax plus by equal to their divisor.
47. The extended Euclidean algorithm finds these coefficients x and y explicitly.
48. Bezout's identity leads directly to a proof of unique prime factorization.
49. A key step is Euclid's lemma about primes dividing products.
50. Euclid's lemma says a prime dividing a product must divide one of the factors.
51. This property fails for composites, since six divides four times nine but neither factor.
52. Modular arithmetic studies integers by focusing only on their remainders.
53. Two integers are congruent modulo n when they leave the same remainder after division by n.
54. Clock arithmetic is a familiar example of working modulo twelve.
55. Seven hours after nine o'clock is four o'clock, since sixteen leaves remainder four.
56. Congruences can be added, subtracted, and multiplied much like ordinary equations.
57. Division is trickier, because not every number has an inverse modulo n.
58. A number has a multiplicative inverse modulo n exactly when it is coprime to n.
59. When n is prime, every nonzero remainder has an inverse.
60. This makes the integers modulo a prime into a structure called a finite field.
61. Fermat's little theorem is a cornerstone result about primes and powers.
62. It says that if p is prime, then a to the p is congruent to a modulo p.
63. Equivalently, a to the power p minus one is congruent to one when p does not divide a.
64. For example, two to the sixth power is sixty-four, which leaves remainder one modulo seven.
65. Fermat's little theorem underlies many quick probabilistic tests for primality.
66. If the congruence fails for some base, the number is definitely composite.
67. Unfortunately, some composite numbers pass the test for every coprime base.
68. These deceptive numbers are called Carmichael numbers in honor of Robert Carmichael.
69. The smallest Carmichael number is five hundred sixty-one, which equals three times eleven times seventeen.
70. There are infinitely many Carmichael numbers, as was proven in nineteen ninety-four.
71. The Miller-Rabin test strengthens Fermat's idea and avoids the Carmichael problem.
72. Each round of Miller-Rabin catches a composite with probability at least three quarters.
73. Running many independent rounds makes the chance of error astronomically small.
74. In two thousand two, researchers found a deterministic polynomial time primality test.
75. That algorithm is known as AKS, after Agrawal, Kayal, and Saxena.
76. Euler's totient function counts the integers up to n that are coprime to n.
77. For a prime p, the totient equals p minus one.
78. For ten, the coprime numbers are one, three, seven, and nine, giving totient four.
79. Euler generalized Fermat's theorem using his totient function.
80. Euler's theorem says a to the totient of n is congruent to one modulo n.
81. This holds whenever a and n are coprime, regardless of whether n is prime.
82. The RSA cryptosystem relies directly on Euler's theorem for its correctness.
83. RSA builds a public key by multiplying two large secret primes together.
84. Anyone can encrypt a message using the public product and an exponent.
85. Decryption requires knowing the totient, which depends on the secret primes.
86. Factoring the product is believed to be extremely difficult for large primes.
87. The security of RSA therefore rests on the apparent hardness of factoring.
88. The Chinese remainder theorem solves systems of congruences with coprime moduli.
89. It guarantees a unique solution modulo the product of those moduli.
90. For example, a number congruent to two mod three and three mod five is eight.
91. The theorem appears in a Chinese text written roughly seventeen centuries ago.
92. It is widely used to speed up computations in modern cryptography.
93. Wilson's theorem offers a curious characterization of prime numbers.
94. It says p is prime exactly when p minus one factorial is congruent to minus one.
95. For five, four factorial is twenty-four, which is one less than twenty-five.
96. Although elegant, Wilson's theorem is useless as a practical primality test.
97. Computing large factorials is far slower than simply performing trial division.
98. Primes become rarer as numbers grow larger, but they never disappear.
99. The prime number theorem describes how primes thin out among the integers.
100. It says the number of primes below x is roughly x divided by its natural logarithm.
101. Hadamard and de la Vallee Poussin independently proved this theorem in eighteen ninety-six.
102. Their proofs used complex analysis and the Riemann zeta function.
103. Near a large number x, about one in every log x integers is prime.
104. Around one million, roughly one number in fourteen is prime.
105. Gaps between consecutive primes can become arbitrarily large.
106. The numbers from n factorial plus two through n factorial plus n are all composite.
107. That gives a run of n minus one consecutive composite numbers.
108. Bertrand's postulate says there is always a prime between n and two n.
109. Chebyshev proved Bertrand's postulate in eighteen fifty-two.
110. Twin primes are pairs of primes that differ by exactly two.
111. Examples of twin primes include three and five, eleven and thirteen, and forty-one and forty-three.
112. Nobody yet knows whether there are infinitely many twin prime pairs.
113. In two thousand thirteen, Yitang Zhang proved that bounded prime gaps occur infinitely often.
114. His initial bound of seventy million was later reduced to two hundred forty-six.
115. Goldbach's conjecture concerns writing even numbers as sums of two primes.
116. It claims every even number greater than two is such a sum.
117. For instance, twenty-eight equals five plus twenty-three and also eleven plus seventeen.
118. The conjecture has been verified by computer for enormously large even numbers.
119. Despite this evidence, a general proof of Goldbach's conjecture remains unknown.
120. Harald Helfgott proved the weak Goldbach conjecture about odd numbers in two thousand thirteen.
121. That result shows every odd number above five is a sum of three primes.
122. Mersenne primes are primes of the form two to the n minus one.
123. For two to the n minus one to be prime, n itself must be prime.
124. The converse fails, since two to the eleventh minus one equals twenty-three times eighty-nine.
125. The largest known primes are almost always Mersenne primes.
126. The Lucas-Lehmer test checks Mersenne numbers for primality very efficiently.
127. The Great Internet Mersenne Prime Search coordinates volunteers hunting for these giants.
128. Record primes discovered this way contain tens of millions of decimal digits.
129. Mersenne primes are closely connected to perfect numbers.
130. A perfect number equals the sum of its proper divisors.
131. Six is perfect, since one plus two plus three equals six.
132. Twenty-eight is also perfect, as its proper divisors sum to twenty-eight.
133. Euclid and Euler together showed even perfect numbers correspond exactly to Mersenne primes.
134. No one knows whether any odd perfect number exists at all.
135. Dirichlet proved that arithmetic progressions often contain infinitely many primes.
136. Specifically, a plus multiples of d contains infinitely many primes when a and d are coprime.
137. So infinitely many primes end in the digit one, three, seven, or nine.
138. Green and Tao showed primes contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions.
139. Their two thousand four theorem combined combinatorics with analytic number theory.
140. Quadratic residues are the perfect squares when reduced modulo a prime.
141. The law of quadratic reciprocity relates residues modulo two different odd primes.
142. Gauss called quadratic reciprocity the golden theorem and proved it several ways.
143. Fermat observed that odd primes congruent to one mod four are sums of two squares.
144. Thirteen illustrates this fact, since it equals four plus nine.
145. Primes congruent to three mod four can never be written that way.
146. The Riemann hypothesis concerns the zeros of the Riemann zeta function.
147. If true, it would sharply control the error in the prime number theorem.
148. It is one of the Millennium Prize Problems carrying a million dollar reward.
149. Primes thus connect simple counting questions with deep and unsolved mysteries.
150. Their study continues to reward both curious beginners and professional mathematicians alike.
